case_analysis.focal_point: Whether plaintiffs can bring a facial or as-applied constitutional challenge to FECA's coordinated party expenditure limits under the First Amendment, given the Supreme Court's prior rejection of such a challenge in FEC v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Committee (Colorado II).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) coordinated party expenditure limits, as challenged under the First Amendment's guarantees of freedom of speech and freedom of association (U.S. Const. amend. I), with procedural framework governed by FECA § 310 and 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Plaintiffs argue that FECA's coordinated party expenditure limits unconstitutionally infringe on their First Amendment rights, contending that Colorado II should no longer govern because: (1) the legal and doctrinal backdrop has materially changed since that decision; (2) they present new arguments not previously raised before the Colorado II court; and (3) subsequent Supreme Court decisions have so thoroughly displaced Colorado II's underlying reasoning that lower courts are no longer strictly bound by it, warranting either an as-applied challenge or outright reconsideration of the precedent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The FEC argues that Colorado II directly and conclusively forecloses the plaintiffs' challenge, as the Supreme Court expressly rejected a facial challenge to the same coordinated expenditure limits on nearly identical factual and legal grounds; that lower courts, as inferior courts under Article III, are bound to follow controlling Supreme Court precedent regardless of perceived doctrinal shifts; and that the district court's role under FECA is limited to findings of adjudicative facts only, with all legal analysis reserved for the court of appeals sitting en banc, making the challenge procedurally improper at the district court level.
